name: Hot comb / straightening comb

card.summary: A heated metal comb drawn through coarse or curly hair to temporarily straighten it from the root for a smooth, sleek look.
card.note: Heat can burn skin and scalp; hot-comb use has historically been discussed in connection with scarring hair loss.

quick.overview:
A hot comb is a metal comb heated on a stove or electrically and passed through hair near the scalp to straighten it. It gives a smooth, straight result that lasts until the hair is wet or the curl returns.

It is closely tied to Black women's hair care in the United States, and to Madam C. J. Walker's business, although historians say she did not invent it.[1]
quick.how: The comb is heated and combed through sectioned hair, usually with a heat-protecting product, as part of a 'press and curl' routine. Results last until the next wash or humidity.
quick.risks: Combs can exceed 65 C (149 F), so burns and scarring are possible. Hot comb alopecia, a scarring hair loss, was named in 1968 for the practice, but later research found a poor link and the condition is now called CCCA.[1][3]

lead: The hot comb, or straightening comb, is a heated metal comb used to straighten moderately to very coarse hair from the roots. It is heated on a stove or electrically.[1]

It was developed in France, where heated irons for waving were introduced by Marcel Grateau in 1872; a US hot comb was later marketed first as a mustache grooming tool. In 1912 a New York salon serving mostly Black women advertised a straightening comb, and Walter Sammons received a US patent in 1920. Madam C. J. Walker is often credited with inventing it, but she bought combs from suppliers such as Louisa B. Cason.[1]
Dermatology literature links the tool's name to 'hot comb alopecia', a scarring hair loss first described in 1968.[2][3]

angle.text: People use it to get straight, smooth hair without chemical relaxers. The straightening is temporary.

paras: Francois Marcel Grateau's 1872 heated irons led to the Marcel wave. In the US, early heated combs were sold for men's mustaches and beards. Straightening-comb advertisements appeared in 1912 and 1915 to 1916, and companies and sellers such as Louisa B. Cason (patent 1922) supplied them. Madam C. J. Walker sold hair-care systems but did not claim to have invented the comb.[1]
The hot comb's history is closely tied to Black women's hair care and to beauty standards in the United States that favoured straightened hair.[1]
Heated combs can burn hair and skin. Petrolatum used with the comb was once thought to cause chronic follicle inflammation.[1]

In 1968 Lopresti described 'hot comb alopecia', later called central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA).[2][3] Later work found it also occurs in people who never used hot combs, and a 1992 study reported a poor link with the tool; causes are considered multifactorial, including genetics and hair-care practices.[1][4]

Reviews of CCCA cover epidemiology, causes and treatment (topical and intralesional steroids, tetracycline antibiotics, hair transplant for refractory cases) and discuss the hot comb's historical role in the condition's name.[4][5] No trials have tested the hot comb as a straightening method.

timeline.event: Marcel Grateau introduces heated irons for waving.[1]
A New York hair emporium advertises a straightening comb.[1]
